Engine powered by steam from boiling water

walkthroughs.body_html:
In 1750 most British people lived in villages. They worked on farms or made cloth at home by hand.

Travel was slow — by horse, on foot, or by boat on rivers and canals. Most things were made one at a time by skilled craftsmen.

Then, between about 1750 and 1900, everything changed. We call this the Industrial Revolution.

The key new technology was the steam engine. Coal was burned to boil water; the steam pushed a piston to power machines.

Thomas Newcomen built an early version in 1712. In the 1760s and 1770s, the Scottish engineer James Watt made a much better one.

Steam could power pumps in mines, machines in factories, trains and ships. Britain had lots of coal and iron — perfect for the new age. 🔥

Instead of working at home, people now went to factories — big buildings full of machines.

In Lancashire, cotton mills spun thread on machines like the spinning jenny and water frame. Workers had to follow strict times and rules.

Towns like Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds grew very fast — this is called urbanisation. 🏭
